stages.title: Reading and writing fundamentals
stages.hook: The letter x is pronounced differently in 'xícara', 'táxi' and 'exemplo'. How can you read Portuguese safely?
explain: Portuguese spelling is quite regular, but some letters have more than one sound. C is like k before a, o, u (casa) and like s before e, i (cinco). G is hard before a, o, u (gato) and soft, like zh, before e, i (gente). Use qu and gu before e or i to keep the hard sound: queijo (cheese), guitarra (guitar). X can sound like sh (xícara), ks (táxi) or z (exemplo).

Stress: words ending in a, e, o, as, es, os, am, em, ens are normally stressed on the second-to-last syllable (casa, falam). Words ending in other letters are stressed on the last syllable (animal, falar). An accent mark shows where the stress breaks the rule: café, você, está. Learn words by listening and reading together.
stages.mnemonic: C and g go soft before e and i; use qu and gu to keep them hard.

gq.why: C is soft before i or e.

gq.q: Why is there a u in 'queijo'?
o: It is pronounced as w in all cases
To keep the k sound before e or i
gq.why: Qu represents k before e and i.

panel.q: A learner pronounces the g in 'gente' as in 'gato'. What is the rule?
o: G is soft (zh) before e and i
panel.why: Soft g appears before e or i.

panel.q: Why does 'café' have an accent mark?
o: The stress is on the last syllable, which is unusual for a word ending in e

panel.q: Which word has x sounding like sh?

teach.model: C and g are soft before e and i. Use qu and gu to keep them hard. X has several sounds. Accent marks show unusual stress.

points.ask: How do c and g work?
What do qu and gu do?
What does an accent mark show?

trip.prompt: See how spelling and sound match.

stages.title: Basic sentence construction
stages.hook: Is the word order in Portuguese the same as in English?
explain: The basic order is subject, verb, object, just like English: 'Eu como pão' (I eat bread). The subject is often dropped because the verb ending shows the person: 'Como pão'. Adjectives usually come after the noun: 'uma casa grande'. To make a negative sentence, put não before the verb: 'Eu não falo inglês'.

Connect ideas with e (and), mas (but), ou (or), porque (because). Prepositions are very common: com (with), sem (without), para (for, to), em (in, on). In sentences, the article shows the gender and number: o livro, os livros, a casa, as casas. Questions keep the same order and use rising intonation: 'Você fala português?'
stages.mnemonic: Subject, verb, object; não before the verb; adjective after the noun.

gq.q: Where does 'não' go in a negative sentence?
How do you say 'a big house'?
gq.why: The adjective normally follows the noun.

panel.q: Why can Portuguese leave out 'eu' in 'Como pão'?
o: The word pão is the subject

panel.q: Which sentence is correct?
How do you make a yes/no question?

teach.model: Order: subject, verb, object. Put não before the verb. Adjectives usually follow the noun. The subject pronoun can be dropped.

points.ask: How do I make a negative?

trip.prompt: Notice how the order of words is similar to English.

stages.title: Common verbs
stages.hook: Portuguese has two verbs for 'to be'. When do you use each?
explain: Ser and estar both mean 'to be'. Ser is for identity and permanent features: 'Eu sou brasileira' (I am Brazilian), 'Ele é alto' (He is tall). Estar is for states, locations and temporary conditions: 'Estou cansado' (I am tired), 'O livro está na mesa' (The book is on the table).

Other key verbs: ter (to have): tenho, tem, temos; ir (to go): vou, vai, vamos; fazer (to do): faço, faz, fazemos; querer (to want): quero. Present of ser: sou, é, somos, são. Present of estar: estou, está, estamos, estão. In Portugal, tu form: tu és, tu estás; in Brazil, você é and você está.
stages.mnemonic: Ser = who you are; estar = how or where you are.

gq.q: Which verb is used for location?

gq.why: Height is a lasting feature, so ser.

panel.q: Why is 'Estou cansado' with estar?
o: Estar is always used with adjectives

panel.q: What changes for 'tu' in European Portuguese?
panel.why: Tu has its own verb forms.

panel.q: What does 'Eu faço o jantar' mean?
panel.why: Fazer is to make or do.

teach.model: Ser is for identity and lasting traits; estar is for states and location. Also learn ter, ir, fazer, querer.

points.ask: What changes between Portugal and Brazil?

stages.title: Nouns, pronouns and modifiers
explain: Most nouns add -s: livro → livros, casa → casas. Nouns ending in -ão have three plurals: -ões (limão → limões), -ães (pão → pães) or -ãos (mão → mãos). Nouns ending in -l change to -is: animal → animais. Nouns ending in -m change to -ns: homem → homens.

Pronouns: eu, tu (in Portugal and parts of Brazil), você, ele, ela, nós, vocês, eles, elas. In Brazil a gente often replaces nós in speech. Contractions: de + o = do, em + a = na, a + o = ao. Demonstratives: este (this), esse (that near you), aquele (that over there).
stages.mnemonic: Limão, limões; pão, pães; mão, mãos.
sentences: The animals are in the garden.

panel.q: Why is it 'no jardim'?
Which pronoun might replace 'nós' in Brazilian speech?
Which demonstrative points to something far from both speakers?

teach.model: Most plurals add -s. Nouns in -ão have three plurals: -ões, -ães, -ãos. Prepositions contract: em + a = na.

points.ask: How do I make a plural?

stages.title: Questions and responses
stages.hook: How do you ask 'Where is the station?' in Portuguese?
explain: Question words: Quem? (Who), O que? (What), Onde? (Where), Quando? (When), Como? (How), Quanto? (How much), Qual? (Which), Por que? (Why). The question 'Onde fica a estação?' means 'Where is the station?' The word 'porque' is also the word for 'because' when answering: 'Por que você estuda português? Porque gosto.'

Yes/no questions keep the same order and use rising intonation: 'Você é do Brasil?' Short answers: Sim (yes), Não (no), Talvez (perhaps), Claro (of course). A tag can be added: 'né?' in Brazil, 'não é?' in Portugal.
stages.mnemonic: Por que? to ask; porque to answer.

gq.q: How do you answer 'Por que você estuda português?'
gq.why: The answer uses porque in one word.

panel.q: Does a yes/no question change word order?
Which question asks the price?
What is 'né?' in Brazil?
panel.why: Né is short for não é.

teach.model: Learn quem, o que, onde, quando, como, quanto, qual, por que. Yes/no questions use rising intonation. Answer with porque.

stages.title: Describing people and places
stages.hook: How would you describe your best friend and your town in Portuguese?
explain: Adjectives agree in gender and number: um menino alto, uma menina alta, meninos altos. Useful words: alto (tall), baixo (short), bonito (beautiful or handsome), simpático (friendly), jovem (young), velho (old), grande (big), pequeno (small). Use ser for lasting features and estar for temporary states: 'Ela é simpática. Ela está feliz hoje.'

Describe places: 'O Rio de Janeiro é uma cidade grande e bonita' (Rio de Janeiro is a big beautiful city). 'Lisboa fica perto do mar' (Lisbon is near the sea). Use 'ter' for what a place has: 'A cidade tem uma praia'. Use 'ficar' to say where something is located in Brazil; 'estar' also works.
stages.mnemonic: Ser for the person; estar for the mood.

gq.q: How do you say 'a tall girl'?

panel.q: Why 'Ela está feliz hoje' with estar?
Is 'jovem' changed for gender?
o: It cannot be used for girls
No, jovem is the same for masculine and feminine
panel.why: Adjectives ending in -em do not change for gender.

panel.q: Which sentence correctly gives a lasting feature?

teach.model: Adjectives agree in gender and number. Use ser for lasting features and estar for temporary states. Jovem and grande have one form for both genders.

stages.title: Time, dates and daily routines
stages.hook: How do you tell the time and the date in Portuguese?
explain: Ask 'Que horas são?' (What time is it?). Answer 'São três horas' (It is three o'clock) but 'É uma hora' (It is one o'clock). 'Meio-dia' is noon and 'meia-noite' is midnight. Days: segunda-feira, terça-feira, quarta-feira, quinta-feira, sexta-feira, sábado, domingo. Months: janeiro, fevereiro, março, abril, maio, junho, julho, agosto, setembro, outubro, novembro, dezembro.

Dates: 'Hoje é dia cinco de maio' (Today is 5 May). Daily routine: acordar (to wake up), tomar café da manhã (Brazil) or tomar o pequeno-almoço (Portugal), almoçar (to have lunch), jantar (to have dinner), dormir. The first day of the week in the calendar is domingo (Sunday).
stages.mnemonic: São três horas, mas é uma hora.
sentences: Today is the fifth of May.

gq.q: How do you say 'It is three o'clock'?

panel.q: Why is it 'É uma hora' and not 'São uma hora'?
Which word do Brazilians use for breakfast?
panel.why: Brazil uses café da manhã; Portugal pequeno-almoço.

panel.q: How do you write days of the week?

teach.model: Que horas são? São três horas; É uma hora. Days and months are in lower case. Breakfast is café da manhã (Brazil) or pequeno-almoço (Portugal).

points.ask: How do I ask the time?

stages.title: Food and shopping
stages.hook: You are in a Brazilian bakery and want a coffee and a pão de queijo. What do you say?
explain: Food words: arroz (rice), feijão (beans), pão (bread), queijo (cheese), leite (milk), frango (chicken), carne (meat), fruta (fruit), café (coffee). Rice and beans are everyday foods in Brazil. In Portugal, the pastel de nata is a famous custard tart.

To order: 'Eu quero um café, por favor' or 'Queria um café, por favor' (polite). To ask the price: 'Quanto custa?' or 'Quanto é?'. To ask for the bill: 'A conta, por favor.' Currencies: real (Brazil), euro (Portugal), kwanza (Angola), metical (Mozambique).
stages.mnemonic: Queria um café, por favor. Quanto é?
sentences: I would like a coffee, please.

gq.q: How do you ask the price?
Which currency is used in Brazil?

panel.q: Why use 'queria' instead of 'quero'?
Which food pair is a Brazilian staple?
What is the plural of 'feijão'?

teach.model: Order with Queria... por favor. Ask the price: Quanto custa? Ask for the bill: A conta, por favor. Currencies: real, euro, kwanza, metical.

points.ask: How do I ask the price?

stages.title: Everyday conversations
stages.hook: What do you say to start a friendly chat with a new classmate?
explain: A short dialogue: 'Oi, tudo bem?' 'Tudo ótimo, e você?' 'Também. Qual é o seu nome?' 'Me chamo Carlos. De onde você é?' 'Sou de Lisboa.' 'Prazer!' Useful words: com licença (excuse me), de nada (you are welcome), desculpe (sorry), claro (of course), tudo bem (all good).

Use 'senhor' and 'senhora' for respect. Brazilians often use 'você'; in Portugal 'tu' with friends and 'o senhor/a senhora' with elders. Saudade is a famous word for a deep feeling of missing someone or something. Gestures and a smile are important.
stages.mnemonic: Oi, tudo bem? Prazer! De onde você é?
sentences: Excuse me, can you help me?

gq.why: De nada is you are welcome.

o: A deep feeling of missing someone

panel.q: Why do speakers use 'senhor' with elders?
Which phrase is used before passing through a crowd?
Which pronoun is used by friends in Portugal?
panel.why: Tu is common among friends in Portugal.

teach.model: Greet with Oi, tudo bem? Ask De onde você é? Say Prazer. Use com licença, de nada, desculpe. Use senhor/senhora with elders.

points.ask: How do I ask where from?
